I have taken @Chillee's dispatch to Python prototype at https://github.com/zou3519/functorch/blob/main/functorch/csrc/PythonKey.cpp and hacked it to a version that doesn't use a PythonTensorImpl holder object. Prototype lives here  master...ezyang:poc-dispatch-to-python
There's a lot of nasty stuff in the prototype that needs to be cleaned up. The purpose of this issue is to describe how the prototype works and describe some of the work that needs to be done.
cc @zou3519 @Chillee @ailzhang
How does holder-less dispatch to Python work
In @Chillee's prototype, an Python object arbitrary is given to addPythonKey which wraps it into an actual Tensor object that can then be passed into PyTorch's dispatcher to have autograd run on it.
In holder-less dispatch to Python, there is no holder object: the Python object subclasses from Tensor, and is directly passed into the bowels of PyTorch. In my prototype, the chain of execution looks like this:

You call torch.add with your Tensor subclass object (whose underlying TensorImpl has the Python dispatch key set)
This dispatches to __torch_function__, where you can immediately override the behavior of the operation prior to the execution of autograd (e.g., to give a custom autograd formula). Let's say you don't want to do that. Then you disable interposition of __torch_function__ at the Python binding layer with torch._C.DisableTorchFunction() (poorly named) and invoke the originally passed in function to enter into the dispatcher (func(*unwrapped_args, **(kwargs if kwargs else {})))
Execution goes through dispatcher, typically passing through Autograd, and then eventually getting to the Python key. The handler then calls back to __torch_function__ again (more on this shortly), via the Python object directly associated with the Tensor object in class.
The __torch_function__ handler handles the primitive operation in question. It's responsible for returning an appropriate tensor subclass for that operation
While unwinding the stack, the Autograd layer will directly modify the returned TensorImpl to set the grad_fn (if necessary). Because this is a mutation, the subclass of the returned tensor is preserved

Construction of subclassed tensors can be done the conventional methods, e.g., using Tensor._make_subclass; all subclass tensor constructors require a real backing tensor.  If you are not actually a CPU/CUDA tensor (but just with extra metadata), then you should use a meta tensor as the backing tensor, as it avoids allocating useless data.
The big open questions
Accidental loss of subclassing.  It is very easy to hit some code path in C++ which ends up "losing" the subclass.  The most common situation this occurs is when options() is used to populate the new subclass, e.g., as seen here:
Tensor new_empty_strided(
    const Tensor& self,
    IntArrayRef size,
    IntArrayRef stride,
    c10::optional<ScalarType> dtype,
    c10::optional<Layout> layout,
    c10::optional<Device> device,
    c10::optional<bool> pin_memory
    ) {
  // See [Note: hacky wrapper removal for TensorOptions]
  TensorOptions options = TensorOptions().dtype(dtype).layout(layout).device(device).pinned_memory(pin_memory);

  return at::empty_strided(size, stride, self.options().merge_in(options));
}

Sometimes, loss of subclassing is harmless, because the subclass in question didn't need to accurately trace the constructor here (empty_strided) and can just trace a constant later.  However, there are a few cases where life is pretty bad:


You construct a tensor, and then copy_ into it from a subclass  (this happens, e.g., in clone_obey_contract which is invoked the first time you accumulate gradients into a variable).  copy_ is not supposed to change the type of the destination, which means you will still have a non-subclass tensor, when you probably actually want one.


The Tensor subclass reports its device type as meta (which is what will happen if you use meta tensors as the backing tensor).  In this case, the initial factory call will generate a meta tensor (losing all data that would be associated with it), and you lose the ability to process the constant later (because meta tensors don't have any data).


These points lead me to suspect that subclassed tensors that are backed by meta tensors should get a custom device type (e.g., torch.device("python")).  This would make it possible for us to directly raise an error when options() is used to directly construct a new type, and force people to rewrite code to not use TensorOptions.  Note that use of TensorOptions inside CPU/CUDA kernels is fine; what's not OK is use of it inside composite kernels (which woudl support Python execution).
Loss of subclass problems are difficult to debug, because typically the invocation that drops the subclass occurs in C++, and the problem isn't discovered until later, so a typical user has no way to debug these problems.  Anomaly mode in autograd can help, but it will only tell you what forward operation is associated with the error in question.
Shallow copy and detach. shallow_copy_and_detach is an operation that was introduced during Tensor-Variable merge and is used to simulate "unwrapping" a variable (e.g., when you write x.data). During regular forward execution, this operation is most typically called when saving variables for backwards (called via SavedVariable).
Now here's the problem: shallow_copy_and_detach is not actually an operation; it's a virtualized method on TensorImpl. And that means it doesn't get intercepted by the Python dispatch key.
In the prototype, I hack around this problem by adding another hook to PyInterpreter to call into Python bindings to propagate the subclass. But it wasn't altogether clear how to implement this correctly (the prototype constructs the new subclass and then copies __dict__ but I bet this is wrong)`. Some of the SavedVariable business will be obviated by @albanD's work on #58500 but I think in some cases it will still be necessary to do a shallow copy and detach.
One thing that isn't too clear to me is what the difference between a detach and a shallow_copy_and_detach. If there is no substantive difference, I'd quite like it if we replaced occurrences of this low level operation with just a regular detach, because then I can report these as detach to __torch_function__ reusing the same API. Does that mean we can delete shallow_copy_and_detach entirely? (But it seems there needs to be a low level API that has access to all the private properties on TensorImpl).

Update 1: The prototype currently translates shallow_copy_and_detach in to detach stock invocations and this all works OK although it looks a little ugly

Should Python dispatch key dispatch to torch function? In the prototype, you hit __torch_function__ twice; once at the preexisting Python dispatch layer, and then a second time from the Python dispatch key. Confusingly, the second dispatch always occurs even after you DisableTorchFunction. Most implementations of __torch_function__ will have to distinguish between these two cases, probably by testing if torch function was already disabled at time of invocation.
An alternate API is to separate the two APIs, so there is a __torch_function__ API and a __torch_post_autograd_function__ API (naming subject to bikeshedding). __torch_function__ can then be omitted if no high level overriding is desired. This is a relatively simple implementation change to make, we just have to decide what we want to do.

Update 1: prototype now does __torch_dispatch__.  This also revealed that the default __torch_function__ implementation isn't quite right, so this will need some adjusting (not done yet)

Easy to fix problems
Python dispatch key must be cleared on TensorImpl construction. In most cases, when a view or shallow copy is made, we propagate the dispatch key set as is.  The Python dispatch key must not be propagated in this way: it attests that the PyObject associated with the Tensor is a subclass with a nontrivial __torch_function__, but of course a newly created TensorImpl has no PyObject associated with it.  The Python dispatch key should be set shortly afterwards when control returns to __torch_function__ and it actually constructs a subclass.

Update 1: This is done in the prototype

Python bindings must work with Autograd/ViewOrInplace disabled. When we call back to Python from the Python dispatch key, the Autograd/ViewOrInplace keys will be disabled. This is a new mode of execution inside Python, where typically these keys are never disabled (as such disabling can only be done from C++). Fortunately, we were already planning to do this, see #54614  https://fb.quip.com/hfSlAZZBnbbp However, there are still some bugs that need to be fixed.
One bug that I observed in particular is that when Autograd/ViewOrInplace is disabled, detach() devolves to an identity function:
Tensor detach(const Tensor& self) {
  // this just exists to give us a hook in VariableType and an entry in Declarations.yaml
  //AT_ERROR("detach is not implemented for Tensor");
  return self;
}

This is wrong. detach must always return a fresh tensor, even without autograd this is part of the API contract for the function. This resulted in a bug in the prototype where make_subclass incorrectly modified the input tensor:
@@ -314,7 +315,8 @@ static PyObject* THPVariable_make_subclass(PyObject* _ignored, PyObject* args, P
     throw torch::TypeError("cls must be a type (got %s)", Py_TYPE(cls)->tp_name);
   }
   auto data =
-      r.tensor(1).detach(); // creates a fresh Tensor (DEFINITELY_UNINITIALIZED)
+      r.tensor(1).detach().alias(); // BLEGHHHH
   // We set `data`'s `allow_tensor_metadata_change` to true here, because we want to
   // allow the following use case for backward compatibility:
   //

P.S. I also don't really have any good idea what detach_ is supposed to do here; it seems like you still should actually clear out the grad_fn even if autograd is disabled.
Tensor & detach_(Tensor & self) {
  // this just exists to give us a hook in VariableType and an entry in Declarations.yaml
  //AT_ERROR("detach_ is not implemented for Tensor");
  return self;
}


Update 1: This is fixed in #59633

Python dispatch key and torchdeploy.  Already tracked at #58864
Shared torch function infrastructure.  When dispatching to __torch_function__ from Python dispatch key, we must properly do all of the type resolution work that regular __torch_function__ at the Python layer does (i.e., if there are multiple Python objects with differing subclasses, pick the most specific one, and then keep trying until someone doesn't return NotImplemented).  This logic isn't easily accessible, so @Chillee did a crappy implementation where he just always dispatched on the first argument. NOT OK.

Update 1: This is fixed in the prototype

Should we populate kwargs? __torch_function__ faithfully replicates what the user call site looked like, so e.g., if you say add(x, y) that will be all positional, but if you say add(x, other=y), you'll get a kwarg for other.  We don't have any call site in the traditional sense in dispatch to Python, so we must make a decision about whether or not put things in kwargs or positional args. The simple choice is to put everything in positional args, but this can be awkward when a function has kwarg-only arguments.

As of #62822 we now populate kwargs for kwarg-only

User guidance: constructing subclasses of Tensors. Ideally, subclasses of tensor could be implemented in this way:
class SubTensor(_C._TensorBase):
    def __init__(self, myarg):
       super().__init__(...something here to say what the sizes/strides/etc should be...)

But actually you can only ever pass no arguments to the super init, because for some reason, it's the generic object constructor:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 7, in <module>
    B()
  File "test.py", line 5, in __init__
    super().__init__(1)
TypeError: object.__init__() takes exactly one argument (the instance to initialize)

Instead, extant uses of subclasses override __new__ and internally use _make_subclass to ensure that the subclass is created:
    @staticmethod
    def __new__(cls, x, *args, **kwargs):
        r = torch.Tensor._make_subclass(cls, x, x.requires_grad)
        r.x = x
        return r

It would be nice to make this more user friendly.

Update (Jun 23): I think this is impossible. __init__ is predicated on our ability to create an otherwise uninitialized Tensor PyObject. To create the PyObject, we must also create the Tensor. And now we are stuck: there is no way to know what Tensor we should create without actually running the constructor.

User guidance: unwrapping and wrapping subclasses.  What does a __torch_function__ that handles inner aten calls (from the dispatch key) look like?  There are two primary variations:


The subclassed tensor is a traditional tensor, plus some extra metadata.  In that case, you'd like to call the "super" implementation directly on the tensor in question, getting back a non-subclassed tensor, and then transform that into a subclass tensor (with whatever extra information you wanted computed in your user code).


The subclasses tensor has a traditional tensor.  In this case, you'd need to unwrap the inputs to get at the traditional tensors, run the algorithm on the result, and then finally wrap a subclass tensor to return as the result.


In the first case, we need the ability to "exclude" Python dispatch key and redispatch (this capability exists but isn't currently bound in Python.  Note that tensors of this form should also have another dispatch key, e.g., a CPU dispatch key attached to themselves!)
In the second case, we need the ability to iterate over input arguments and output returns to wrap/unwrap tensors.  This is boilerplate code that is easy to write incompletely (because, e.g., you might handle tensors but not lists of tensors).  See also pytorch/functorch#43 pytorch/functorch#4  Furthermore, when rewrapping tensors, you also need to construct a tensor of the correct size/shape that you will call _make_subclass on; you may directly construct a meta tensor, or convert one of the wrapped inner tensors into a meta tensor to pass in (this is what the prototype does).
User guidance: it's difficult to turn a subclass back into a normal class. Given a Tensor, I can turn it into a TensorSubclass by calling _make_subclass. How can I turn the TensorSubclass back into a Tensor? Many of the usual suspects don't work:

_make_subclass(subtensor)
Tensor(subtensor)

In an upcoming prototype revision, this will work to convert tensors back:
        with no_dispatch():   
            y = x.detach()

but perhaps we will want a more concise way to do this.
torch.ops don't accept tensor subclasses. I added a guard to exclude Python dispatch key so you can defer to the underlying operation. But this doesn't work with torch.ops.aten which refuse to recognize tensor subclasses as regular tensors.
backward() doesn't put the scalar on the correct device. Have to write y.backward(LoggingTensor(torch.ones(1))), y.backward() doesn't work (it tries to shove a CPU tensor through which will fail unless your __torch_dispatch__ implementation advertises that it can work with mixed devices.

Add support for torch.nn.Module to be used in functional style.
This RFC proposes a design for #49171
Motivation & Pitch
The following points were originally written by @albanD
The goal would be to be able to use nn.Module in two new context that are currently very tricky:
the high level autograd API. Currently, this kind of hack is needed:

               Deletes the attribute specified by the given list of names. 
        

        
          
               For example, to delete the attribute obj.conv.weight,

Extracts the module parameters with their names. (The module will be empty), but the parameters are converted to regular tensors
Creates a new forward function that loads these parameters back and just runs the regular forward pass, but they are loaded as tensors for the forward to work, not as parameters.

Example pseudocode of how to utilize this:
model = MyCoolTorchModule()  # This is a module that holds parameters

def get_functional_module(module):
    tensors, names = _recursive_remover(module)
    # Parameters have been deleted
    assert len(model.parameters()) == 0
    def functional_fwd(*new_params):
       # helper function that sets the parameters back
       _recursive_adder(module, names, new_params)
       return module.forward(inputs)
    return tensors, function

parameters, model_fn = get_functional_module(model)

# Functional use of the above
grad_fn = torch.functional_api.grad(model_fn)
gradn_fn(parameters, inputs)
The current approach shows the following drawbacks

Needs to remove the module parameters
Does not restore them, once the module gets its parameters removed then it won’t be able to be used as a regular module again. state_dict and other functions relying on module parameters won’t work.
Needs to maintain state for a single model in different places
External objects and functions will access torch.nn.Module internals. Not clean

Proposal
Add a torch.nn.Module.functional() method similar to .eval() and .train().

The module will manage its own status without having an external class/function
Accessing its internals
torch.nn.Module becomes big & difficult to maintain.
Allows to convert back/from functional state a single model
Adding another mode to torch.nn.Module requires to deal with 3 possible configurations and switches between them. eval/train/functional, this can lead to issues and be a potential no-compat for user-defined modules
Overhead of setting the parameters back and from every iteration can be high.
If the  parameters that are passed functionally to the module are not views of the original parameters, in-place updates to these will not have any effect on the current module state

# torch/nn/module.py

class _FunctionalState:
    def __init__(self, parameters):
        self._names, self._parameters = list(parameters)
    def __iter__(self):
        return self
    def __next__(self):
        for n, p in zip(self._names, self._parameters):
            yield n, p

class Module:

    def functional(functional=True):
       # helper function that sets a hook to replace the parameters
       # pre and after the forward
       func_state = None
       def pre_hook(self, module, inputs):
           nonlocal func_state
           func_state = _FunctionalState(self.named_parameters())    
           # assume that parameters are the first n entries of inputs
           for name, param in zip(func_state._names, inputs):
               module._replace_param(name, param)

       def after_hook(self, module, inputs, outputs):
           for name, param in func_state:
               module._replace_param(name, param)
       if functional:
           self._func_pre_hook = self.register_forward_pre_hook(pre_hook)
           self._func_hook = self.register_forward_hook(after_hook)
       else:
           self._func_pre_hook.remove()
           self._func_hook.remove()
       # return parameters as tensors
       return tuple(p.detach().requires_grad_() for p in self.parameters())


# Functional use of the above
model = MyCoolTorchModule()
parameters = model.functional()
jvp_fn = torch.functional_api.jvp(model)
jvp_fn(parameters, inputs)
If extending module is not acceptable, we can implement a similar solution in a wrapper class

     def __init__(self, module):

           self.func_state = None

               # assume that parameters are the first n entries of inputs
               for name, param in zip(module.func_state._names, inputs):

           def after_hook(self, module, inputs, outputs):
               for name, param in module.func_state:
                   module._replace_param(name, param)
           self._func_pre_hook = self.register_forward_pre_hook(pre_hook)
           self._func_hook = self.register_forward_hook(after_hook)

🚀 Feature

PyTorch has log_softmax and softmax. I am doing a RL agent and I do not care about calculating the log probabilities, just the regular ones with which to sample from. But I'd like to pass the rewards through the log_softmax on the backwards pass. As it happens, the log_softmax's backward function does not require the log probabilities, just the regular ones.
Motivation

Optimizing performance, memory use and code cleanliness.
Pitch

Extend softmax so it takes a flag whether it should act as the log_softmax on the backward pass.
Alternatives

Right now I am going to have to either use the regular softmax and log it later just to pass the gradients through that, or I am going to have to use the log_softmax and then exp it to get the actual probability distribution from which to sample from. I am going to go with later as I anticipate it being more numerically stable, but I do not like the either option.

nn.SmoothL1Loss expects the targets to be of dtype torch.float32. However, if you, for instance, pass targets that are torch.int64, nn.SmoothL1Loss will not complain until until you call loss.backward(). def find_free_port():

    import socket

    with closing(socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)) as s:
        s.bind(('', 0))
        s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        return str(s.getsockname()[1])

def setup_process(opts, rank, world_size, master_port, backend='gloo'):
    """
    Initialize the distributed environment (for each process).

    gloo: is a collective communications library (https://github.com/facebookincubator/gloo). My understanding is that
    it's a library/API for process to communicate/coordinate with each other/master. It's a backend library.

    export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0
    export NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1

    https://stackoverflow.com/questions/61075390/about-pytorch-nccl-error-unhandled-system-error-nccl-version-2-4-8

    https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#common-environment-variables
    """
    import torch.distributed as dist
    import os
    import torch
    # import builtins
    # print2 = functools.partial(print, flush=True); builtins.print = print2
    print(f'setup_process has rank={rank}')

    if is_running_parallel(rank):
        print(f'----> setting up rank={rank} (with world_size={world_size})')
        # MASTER_ADDR = 'localhost'
        MASTER_ADDR = '127.0.0.1'
        MASTER_PORT = master_port
        # set up the master's ip address so this child process can coordinate
        os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = MASTER_ADDR
        print(f"---> {MASTER_ADDR=}")
        os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = MASTER_PORT
        print(f"---> {MASTER_PORT}")

        # - use NCCL if you are using gpus: https://pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/dist_tuto.html#communication-backends
        if torch.cuda.is_available():
            # https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/54550 You need to call torch.cuda.set_device(rank) before init_process_group is called.
            backend = 'nccl'
            torch.cuda.set_device(opts.device)  # is this right if we do parallel cpu?
        print(f'---> {backend=}')
        # Initializes the default distributed process group, and this will also initialize the distributed package.
        dist.init_process_group(backend, rank=rank, world_size=world_size)
        print(f'----> done setting up rank={rank}')
        torch.distributed.barrier()

    """ Destroy a given process group, and deinitialize the distributed package """

    if is_running_parallel(rank):

🐛 Bug
The get_socket_with_port() api gets a free port bound to the "localhost" interface. This is a loopback interface.
create_c10d_store() is being a passed a servername (socket.gethostname()), which returns "localhost" if no hostname is assigned.
If a hostname is assigned, then the that name is being passed to create_c10d_store(). The problem is this hostname is assigned an actual interface IP, instead of the loopback one.
Hence in this test, the original port blocked is on the localhost loopback interface, but the c10d_store is getting a port from a proper IP assigned interface.
Normally this would pass if the servers did not have any assigned hostname. Then get_host_name() would return "localhost".

🚀 Feature
#58224 is adding a ProcessGroupWrapper class, that, at a high level adds consistency checks around collective calls when debug mode is enabled. Currently, we verify operation types and tensor shapes, but this requires a couple of different allgather calls to ensure everything is consistent.
Instead, as proposed by @zhaojuanmao, we can:


right now we are verifying operation type and tensor shapes only, and for each check we need to create a separate tensor and call all gather separately
could we build a meta struct like 'struct collectiveSignature {operation type; tensor size; tensor shape; tensor type; tensor device...}', then serialize this struct into binary tensor, all gather the binary tensor and check whether the binary tensor is matched or not
if the binary signature tensor is not matched, the error message can just simply log the 'struct collectiveSignature()', so that users know which part is wrong
In this way, only one tensor and one all gather needs to be called no matter how much meta info we want to check, also it will be easier to add new meta info we want to check in the future


This will also enable us to check additional data that should be consistent (tensor type, device) that we currently don't check.
